Title: Old lessons and new challenges
text: OLD LESSONS AND NEW CHALLENGES Speech by dr. Jan Marc Berk, Deputy Director Monetary Policy of the Monetary and economic policy department of the Nederlandsche Bank, for the conference on Economic policy directions in the OECD countries: analysing the experiences Warsaw, 21-22 March 2002 (SLIDE 1).  Introduction Monetary policy is an art. There is no universally accepted method for conducting monetary policy that will ensure always and everywhere success. However, this does not mean that artists cannot learn from each other. It is from this perspective that I would like to share with you our experiences in fighting inflation in the seventies and eighties, both from a national and EU perspective. This will entail some reflection on past monetary policy practices, on their successes, but also on the policy errors of the past. Making errors is human. The important thing is that we learn from them. Armed with these experiences, I will also discuss some of the major policy challenges facing accession countries today, from the perspective of an outsider of course.  Fighting inflation in the seventies and eighties To put the fight against inflation in Europe in the 1970s and 1980s in perspective, it is useful to make a quick comparison between the European Union then and the accession countries now (SLIDE 2). Cpi-inflation in the accession countries has been substantially higher than in the European Union roughly 25 years ago. The present-day situation shows that inflation in accession countries, although reduced considerably, still exceeds EU inflation figures by a wide margin. Real GDP-growth in the accession countries is also higher, reflecting the catching-up process. At the same time unemployment is a bigger problem in the accession countries. This brief overview shows that the two cases are not identical, reflecting differences in the underlying causes of inflation and the different state of economic development. Therefore, the lessons from inflation fighting in the EU clearly do not provide a complete blueprint for the accession countries, as these will have to deal with challenges that are different to the earlier experiences of the industrial countries. In the 1970s and 1980s, the EU countries faced two episodes of severe inflation, one in the mid-seventies and the other around the beginning of the eighties (SLIDE 3). The causes are well known. When the first oil price shock hit the world economy in 1973, many industrialised countries were at their cyclical peak. Capacity constraints already exerted upward pressure on wages and prices. Following the sharp rise in oil prices, the world went into a deep recession while inflation accelerated. The monetary policy response to counter the oil price shock varied across countries, as did their inflation rates. Most European countries, including the Netherlands, chose to pursue generally accommodative monetary and fiscal policies. As a result, output and employment rebounded, but so did inflation. In contrast, Germany generally maintained a restrictive monetary policy stance, limiting the inflationary impact of the oil price rise to only the direct first round effect. German consumer price inflation subsequently returned quickly to relatively low levels. The rapid rebound of economic growth in Europe masked a number of structural problems. These became painfully clear when the second round of oil price increases caused another inflationary shock in 1979. Macroeconomic policies were not as accommodative as they were earlier in the decade, resulting in a disinflationary process that entailed significant costs in terms of output and employment. Europe learnt the importance of a flexible economy the hard way. Although Germanys successful move to monetary targeting in 1974 was followed by a number of other countries (such as France in 1977), it did not always stabilise inflation expectations. Following the limited success of the European snake arrangement of exchange rate linkages, the European Monetary System, EMS, was established in 1979, in a second attempt to provide exchange rate stability. Although initially marred by repeated exchange rate adjustments, it was more successful from the early eighties onwards as countries shifted to explicit exchange rate targeting. This helped to discipline domestic macro-economic policies. The success of the EMS was based on the credible determination of Germany to give high priority to the objective of domestic price stability. This was reflected in both actual policy actions and institutional arrangements, including the independent position of the Bundesbank. German monetary policy thus functioned as an anchor of stability for other European countries, which had to accept the consequences for domestic policy if they wished to maintain exchange rate stability. These dilemmas were most pronounced in periods of external turbulence. Examples of the latter include those caused by the volatility of the US dollar, or of asymmetric shocks like the German unification. Each time the US dollar was weak, tensions arose in the EMS and pressure was exerted, unsuccessfully, on the German Bundesbank to lower interest rates. In the Netherlands we experienced these issues as well, albeit on a different scale than some of the larger countries.  Dutch experiences After the demise of the Bretton Woods system, the Netherlands has always participated in exchange rate arrangements, which sought to stabilise intra-European exchange rates. This was deemed to be particularly important for an open economy such as the Netherlands. In the snake arrangement and later in the EMS the Deutsche mark became the nominal anchor for Dutch monetary policy. The Dutch motivation for pegging the exchange rate vis-a-vis the Deutsche mark was twofold. First, a stable exchange rate with the main trading partner Germany fostered trade. Second, Germany was a country with a very good track record of fighting inflation. By credibly pegging its exchange rate to the Deutsche mark, the Netherlands actually could import this excellent reputation (SLIDE 4). More generally, aiming at exchange rate stabilisation was consistent with the creation of the common European market. Since 1983, the Netherlands has formed a de facto monetary union with Germany, until the irrevocable fixing of European exchange rates at the start of EMU. During this period, exchange rate fluctuations of the guilder against the Deutsche mark have been very limited, while the interest rates in the two countries moved virtually in parallel. The Dutch exchange rate peg with the Deutsche mark has sometimes been put forward by accession countries as an illustration of successful disinflation via exchange rate stabilisation. Indeed, the Dutch exchange rate peg was a successful one, not least so because the Netherlands had pegged its exchange rate to a currency of a country it was structurally converged to. Because of structural similarities and synchronised business cycles, German interest rates were also suitable for us. As such, the Dutch pegging experience is probably not the best example for the accession countries. However, this happy state of affairs did not come about by itself. We had our share of problems. Let me briefly cite one. During the 1970s and early eighties, the Netherlands was plagued by an asymmetric shock commonly known as the Dutch disease. The cause was the discovery and exploration of large natural gas deposits. This exploration led to relatively high productivity growth in the energy sector and corresponding wage increases. Due to centralised wage bargaining and indexation mechanisms, wages in non-energy sectors rose as well, but these were not matched by higher productivity growth. The ensuing rise in unit labour costs caused upward pressure on inflation and resulted in a wage-price spiral. These developments are to some extent similar to the well-known Balassa-Samuelson effect. In addition, the export revenues of natural gas implied a windfall gain for the government, which it neglected to use for the strengthening of the economic structure. Instead, much was spent on improvement of the social security system. In a now-famous tripartite accord among the government, trade unions and the employers organisations, a policy of wage moderation and fiscal discipline was agreed in exchange for a shortening of the workweek (SLIDE 5). The credible fixation of the Dutch guilder to the German Mark contributed to the establishment of this agreement, as it provided the right environment for disciplining the economy. The aim was to restore a sound fiscal position, bring inflation down and, above all, create jobs. As a result, the Dutch disease was turned into a Dutch miracle, and the Dutch economy outperformed the European average during the 1990s, although unit labour costs have risen lately.  Old lessons Now, what can we learn today from these earlier experiences? A general lesson is that monetary accommodation of an adverse supply shock should be limited in order to prevent inflationary expectations from rising and second round effects from occurring. Ultimately, an accommodative monetary policy in response to an adverse supply shock is not a viable substitute to real adjustment. A lesson we draw from the Dutch experience is that monetary policy cannot be conducted in an economic vacuum. Monetary policy should be complemented with sound fiscal policy and a greater flexibility of product and labour markets. But a credible monetary policy can be a disciplining device for other policymakers. (SLIDE 6) It is fair to say that the accession countries have already incorporated many of the earlier lessons learned. Most importantly, monetary policy is geared towards medium-term price stability and central banks have worked hard to establish credibility. Nevertheless, accession to the European Union, and ultimately the adoption of the euro, pose significant additional policy challenges for the countries of Central and Eastern Europe. Therefore, lets leave the separated past behind and focus on our shared future of an enlarged European Union.  New challenges Accession countries still undergo far-reaching structural adjustments in their economies. These pose major monetary policy challenges. Let me start with the process of bringing down inflation further. There are a number of factors that work against this process. Disinflation challenge number one is the inevitability of a real appreciation. Convergence requires a stronger economic growth performance in the accession countries compared to the European Union. The difference between the average purchasing power per capita in the accession countries versus the EU gives an indication of the level of price convergence that will need to occur (SLIDE 7). Countries like Poland and the Czech Republic would need to grow by 11% per annum on average for the next twenty years in order to reach the average income per capita of Portugal, Spain and Greece. A successful process of catching up and bridging the price and income differentials will eventually lead to a substantial appreciation of the real exchange rate. Although part of the real appreciation could proceed through a nominal appreciation of the exchange rate, it is likely to coincide with higher inflation levels. Other challenges for the accession countries include how to deal with capital inflows and asymmetric shocks. Improved investment opportunities in maturing transition economies with liberalised financial markets typically attract foreign capital inflows. While foreign direct investment is conducive to enhancing economic growth, volatile short-term capital flows pose challenges to exchange rate policy, especially in a fixed exchange rate regime. Furthermore, countries with an overexposure to a few sectors, or a high dependency on foreign capital inflows could be exposed to asymmetric shocks, making it hard to pursue a stable exchange rate and a disinflation. In a way, European Union membership itself might be a kind of an asymmetric shock, given its strong direct effect on competitiveness and policy-making. When asymmetric shocks occur, adjustments must be made in the domestic economy. This requires the adjustment of relative price levels, depending on the availability of flexible labour markets, including wage setting. In such an uncertain environment, exchange rate flexibility can offer a helping hand in stabilising economic conditions. I do not, however, prescribe exchange rate flexibility as the ultimate panacea. Flexible and pegged exchange rate regimes have both merits and disadvantages. They differ in how the costs of real adjustment, that have to be paid in any case, are distributed. Ultimately, the choice of regime depends on the circumstances in each country at a given point in time.  Euro adoption A number of governments and central bankers of accession countries have expressed their preference for an early adoption of the euro. In principle, their motivation for adopting the euro is the same as was the case for the current euro participants (SLIDE 8). However, as accession countries make up only around seven percent of EU GDP, the monetary stance of the Eurosystem could be systematically out of line with their needs, particularly during the first years. A high growth and inflation environment could result in strong wage pressures and erode competitiveness in the accession countries. In a worst case scenario, negative real interest rates could emerge, leading to boom-bust cycles. And possibly asset price bubbles, given the relatively underdeveloped financial markets. A premature focus on euro adoption might actually slow down the process of catching up. The Maastricht criteria were created for countries that had already converged significantly in structural terms. Tight fiscal and monetary policies in the accession countries to meet the inflation criterion might come at the expense of actual income convergence. In addition, necessary investments in human capital and the restructuring of heavy industries might be postponed to meet the deficit criterion. All this is certainly not to deny that many accession countries have done exceptionally well in stabilising their economies. In fact, some do even better on the Maastricht criteria than a number of the current euro-members did in the early nineties. Key message, however, is that EMU membership should be carefully considered as a three-stage approach. Currently, the focus should be EU accession. Afterwards, further convergence should take place, in which participation in the European exchange rate mechanism may offer a helpful combination of stability and flexibility. Finally, when the conditions are right and a high degree of sustainable convergence is achieved, euro-adoption will follow. Title: Report on the implementation of monetary policy assumptions in 2002
text: Warsaw, 23 July 2003 Speech by Leszek Balcerowicz, President of the National Bank of Poland, in the parliamentary debate on the Report on the implementation of the monetary policy assumptions in 2002 and the Report on the activities of the National Bank of Poland in 2002 I 1. Introduction. 1.1. Benefits of price stability. Mr Speaker, Honourable Members, As you know, money makes it possible to fundamentally expand the scope of exchange and thus radically increase the well-being of society. Money also allows you to quickly get an idea of the values of individual dr and makes it easier to store value. But money actually fulfills these important functions only when it itself retains value, and therefore - when prices are stable. Excessive price increases make people less willing to accept money in exchange for goods. Prices expressed in money cease to reflect well the value of individual drs, because some prices adjust faster and others slower to the increased mass of money. Finally, money ceases to be a good store of value, because with the passage of time less and less commodities can be bought for the same amount of money. High inflation relegates the developed economy to the state of a primitive economy. At this point, let me quote the words of John Maynard Keynes: Lenin was right. No has a more perfidious or more reliable method to overthrow the foundations of society's existence than the corruption of money. This process unleashes all the hidden forces of the laws of economics, engaging them on the side of destruction, and does so in a way that even one man in a million is unable to recognize. Awareness of the benefits of price stability and the harms of high inflation is reflected in paragraph 1 of Article 227 of our Constitution. It imposes on the National Bank of Polish the obligation to take care of the value of Polish money, i.e. that it does not lose its purchasing power and fog  thanks to which it serves the development of the economy well. *** In September 1998, the Monetary Policy Council, guided by the Constitution, adopted as a strategic objective of monetary policy to bring inflation below 4% in 2003. In order to achieve this, the Council announced supporting objectives every year. In August 2001, the inflation target for 2002 was adopted. It was set at 5% with a deviation range of /-1 percentage point. In June 2002, the Monetary Policy Council reduced it to 3% with the same range of deviations. Inflation at the end of 2002 was 0.8%, which was lower than the annual inflation target. Such a deviation obviously needs to be explained 1.2. Factors limiting hitting the inflation target. Mr Speaker, Honourable Members, Even in high-income countries with years of low inflation, price growth often deviates from the inflation target. Last year, for example, in the eurozone, only in June inflation was in the range of 0-2%, which was set by the inflation target of the European Central Bank. Inflation deviates from the inflation target mainly because the increase in prices, especially the end line, is influenced not only by the policy of the central bank, but also by factors that are not influenced by it and which are difficult to predict. The price level may unexpectedly change as a result of temporary changes in supply, e.g. from grain or crude oil. The Monetary Policy Assumptions for 2002 clearly indicate that such risks exist. It is much more difficult to achieve the inflation target in low-income countries, where spending on products whose supply is most unpredictable accounts for a high percentage of total household spending. As a result, changes in the prices of such dr strongly affect the inflation rate. In Poland, food prices alone account for almost 30 per cent of inflation, while in the United States it is less than 16 per cent, in Switzerland less than 12 per cent, and in the eurozone including alcoholic beverages and tobacco products about 19 per cent. Therefore, every year the list of low-income countries that have not reached their inflation target is very long. Here are just a few examples from last year:  in Brazil, the inflation target was set at 3.5% with a deviation range of /-2 percentage points, and prices increased by 12.5%;  in Israel, the inflation target was set at 2-3 per cent, and inflation was 6.5 per cent;  in the Czech Republic, on the other hand, the inflation target was between 3%and 5%, and inflation fell to 0.6%. In addition, it is more difficult to hit the inflation target when inflation is lowered to a low level than when it is stabilized at that level. In the first case, as until the end of 2002 in Poland, it is necessary to set auxiliary, annual inflation targets, and such goals are more difficult to hit than continuous ones. Higher inflation is subject to much greater fluctuations than low inflation. As a result, it is much easier to make a mistake when forecasting the future level of inflation, which has yet to be lowered. This is because central banks in countries that have been allowed to experience high inflation in the past have yet to build their credibility. It is more difficult for them than in countries with stable prices to convince people that they do not have to demand a rapid increase in wages or higher prices for the products they sell in order to preserve the purchasing power of their income. When you can't accurately predict what percentage of people will trust assurances that inflation reduction is possible, it's not hard to get it wrong to set an annual inflation target. Achieving the auxiliary annual inflation targets is also difficult because between changes in percentages and their effects visible in the economy occur large delays, which in the case of prices reach 6 and more quarters. Because of these delays, the central bank has little opportunity to hit its annual inflation target when large, unforeseen changes in the supply of some products occur during the year. In order to significantly mitigate the impact of these unexpected changes on inflation, the bank would have to rapidly change the level of st percent so that the prices of other companies would deviate in the opposite direction. But such behavior, instead of reducing, would increase uncertainty in the economy. An increase in uncertainty would in turn increase the risk that, by reaching the target in one year, the central bank would increase the risk that the strategic objective of achieving price stability would not be achieved. In addition, changes in supply are usually reversible after an exceptional harvest, there are periods of average harvest or even crop failure; the increase in oil prices prompts many countries to increase its production, and their decrease to limit it. There is therefore a high probability that during the period of time, which is needed for the effects of the changes in percentages to become visible in the economy, the direction of changes in supply, and thus their impact on prices, would be reversed. For all these reasons, the Monetary Policy Council, when announcing the inflation target for 2002, at the same time strongly emphasized that the implementation of this goal is less important than the strategic goal. 1.3. Conditions under which the inflation target for 2002 was set and revised. In mid-2001, i.e. before the announcement of the inflation target at the level of 5% with a deviation range of /- 1 percentage point, the average of inflation forecasts for the end of 2002, prepared by analytical centres and banks, was about 5.3%. No research center or institution, either in Poland or abroad, predicted inflation for 2002, which would be lower than the lower limit of deviations from the inflation target. This also applies to all government centers. On the other hand, there were those who predicted inflation higher than 6 percent, i.e. the limit of deviations from this goal. Not only the forecasts, but also the inflation expectations of households were high - people expected prices to increase by about 6% during the year. The economic situation in the first half of 2002 was much more conducive to lowering inflation than anyone had predicted. In June of the same year, the Monetary Policy Council lowered the inflation target to 3% with a deviation range of /-1 percentage points. I must take this opportunity to correct the rapporteur's false information that the MPC did not inform the government about the change of purpose beforehand. I have here before me an appropriate letter to the Prime Minister on this matter. The aim of the change was to avoid misinterpretations as to the direction of monetary policy, or more precisely to eliminate the assumption that it would strive at all costs to achieve the inflation target set in mid-2001 at the expense of the strategic objective. The revised inflation target for 2002 was in line with tuition forecasts inflation of all I repeat all - well-known analytical centers. Nobody then he did not anticipate that inflation would fall below the lower limit of deviations from the revised target. Some argued that the Council had lowered its inflation target too much. 2. The sources of inflation in 2002. In 2002, the prices of all major groups of consumer goods and services grew more slowly than the year before. The reduction in inflation was therefore not only due to unforeseen changes on the supply side and administrative prices. However, these two factors fully explain 100% - the fall in inflation below the inflation target. 2.1. The main factors explaining the failure to hit the inflation target. 2.1.1. Food prices. This reduction in inflation was partly due to an unforeseen fall in food prices. Last year, they decreased by 2.7 percent, while a year earlier they increased by 1.6 percent, and in 2000 - by as much as 8.5 percent. This illustrates the scale of fluctuations in this important price category. On the basis of information coming mainly from the Central Statistical Office, the Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics and the Agricultural Market Agency, available in June 2002, the National Bank of Polish predicted that food prices would increase by 2.6% in 2002. If food prices had risen in 2002 at the rate forecasted or as in In 2001, inflation would have exceeded 2 per cent, which would have been within the limits of the inflation target. 2.1.2. Controlled prices. The slower growth of administered prices also contributed to the decline in inflation below the inflation target. In 2002, they increased by 2.7 per cent, while according to the NBP forecast prepared in June 2002, they were to increase by 4.5 per cent. The increase in administered prices turned out to be weaker as a result of an unexpected, deep reduction in excise duty on alcoholic beverages, which was not in the budget assumptions, a lower than expected scale of increases in energy and gas tariffs, as well as a weaker than expected impact of excise duty on electricity prices. Had the June 2002 food and administered price projections been correct, inflation at the end of 2002 would have been around 2.8%, i.e. within the limits of the inflation target. The increase in the prices of other goods and services amounted to 2.1 percent, so it was within these limits. 2.2. Other selected factors influencing inflation in 2001 2.2.1. External environment and inflation. These two factors, an unforeseen decline in food prices and a weaker-than-expected increase in administered prices, are sufficient to explain the fall in inflation below the inflation target. But there was also a third factor, namely - the growth of the world economy in 2002 turned out to be much slower than anyone predicted. In mid-2001, the International Monetary Fund, the OECD and the European Commission predicted that GDP growth in the eurozone would be 2.7-2.9% in 2002, including 2.4-2.6% in Germany. If these forecasts came true, economic growth in our country would gain additional impulses. It would be much easier to sell Polish goods abroad, and this in turn could encourage our companies to undertake new investments. This assumed improvement in the economic situation also allowed us to expect a stronger increase in prices. There would be a greater demand in the global economy for raw materials, and thus higher prices. In turn, the growing demand for Polish goods would create opportunities for our companies to raise prices for manufactured products without the risk of losing the customer. However, 2002 did not bring the expected improvement in the world economy. The forecasts of the International Monetary Fund, the OECD and the European Commission available in June 2002, when the Monetary Policy Council changed its inflation target, were in the range of 1.3-1.4% for the eurozone and 0.7-0.9% for Germany. The actual results turned out to be even worse, despite the decrease in Western countries. percentages to a record low. GDP in 2002 increased by 0.8% in the eurozone and by only 0.2% in Germany. 3. Monetary policy. 3.1. Monetary policy 2001-2002. Thank you, Mr Marshal. High Chamber! Monetary policy contributed to the consolidation of inflation at a low level in 2002, not only this year but also earlier. There are large delays between changes in percentages and their effects in the economy. So it is necessary to recall the facts, which are easily forgotten. From February 1999 to July 2000, inflation rose from less than 6 percent to nearly 12 percent. People have adjusted their expectations to rising inflation. As recently as April 1999, they predicted that prices would rise by 6% within a year, and in August 2000 they raised these expectations to 12%. In order to counteract the spiral of growth in inflation expectations, wages and prices, the Monetary Policy Council raised THE NBP interest rates by a total of 2.5 percentage points in 2000. This allowed to slow down the dangerous growth of inflation expectations and inflation itself. Since February 2001, NBP interest rates have changed only in one direction and have been gradually reduced. By the end of 2002, the Monetary Policy Council had made fourteen reductions (six in 2001 and eight in 2002). The reference rate, the most important of the NBP percentages, fell from 19 to 6.75 percent. In this way, nominal NBP interest rates were at the lowest level since the early nineties. Real rates, i.e. adjusted for inflation, also fell. From the first reduction in interest rates, made in February 2001, to the end of last year, the reference rate after deducting inflation has fallen by almost half, and in 2002 alone by more than a fifth. Last year, monetary conditions were further eased by the weakening of the zloty exchange rate. During the whole year, it was on average about 4% weaker in relation to the currencies of the most important trading partners of our country than in the previous year. This year, the Monetary Policy Council continued to lower interest rates. In total, since February 2001, the Council has made 20 reductions, reducing the reference rate from 19 to 5.25 percent, or 13.75 percentage points. At the same time, in the Czech Republic, the central bank reduced its main interest rate by 3 percentage points, and in Hungary and Slovakia - by 1.5 percentage points. 3.2. Indications of caution in reducing percentages. 3.2.1. Costs of too deep a reduction in percentages. Mr Speaker, Honourable Members, Interest rates in Poland were lowered in such a way as to prevent people from becoming afraid of a rapid increase in prices and, as a result, wanting to protect themselves against it, increase their wage demands or raise prices, which they have an impact on. There is no shortage of countries in which there was a recurrence of inflation, and it seemed that the fight against it was a definite success. A recent example is Israel. The Bank of Israel's main interest rate fell from 13.5 percent in February 1999 to 5.8 percent in December 2001. With inflation at 1.4 percent, the central bank cut the rate by 2 percentage points in one fell swoop. Two months later, in order to slow down the increase in inflation, he had to raise interest rates again by a total of 5.3 percentage points over the next 5 months. The increase in inflation was stopped only when it reached 7 percent. Another example is Hungary. At the beginning of June this year, the Hungarian central bank weakened the forint its central parity - by 2.26 percent. This has sparked speculation that such decisions could be made again in the future. The forint began to depreciate rapidly. The National Bank of Hungary has taken a step forward by raising interest rates by 1 percentage point. But the following week, a billion dollars were withdrawn from the Hungarian bond market. This forced the central bank to raise the percentages by another 2 percentage points. Currently, the main rate of the National Bank of Hungary is 9.5 percent, i.e. the same as a year earlier. At the same time, there were concerns that inflation could turn out to be higher than expected. These examples show, I think, how important caution in central bank policy is to consolidate low inflation. Doing the opposite usually only entails costs, contributing nothing to the growth of the economy. But even if the central bank were able to temporarily stimulate the economy without risk, the benefit for households would be negligible in terms of the benefits of price stability. It is worth quoting the estimates of Robert Lucas, a prominent American economist, Nobel prize winner. They show that the benefits of a sustained reduction in inflation from 10% to zero may be up to twenty times greater than the benefits of eliminating cyclical fluctuations in economic activity. And this is how much inflation in Poland has fallen since July 2000. 3.2.2. Rapid deterioration of the state finances. Mr. Marshal, High Sejm! The room for manoeuvre in monetary policy has been severely narrowed by the bad situation in the sphere of state finances. The high budget deficit increases the risk of rising inflation.  Firstly, expenditures excessive in relation to the financial capacity of the state, i.e. the deficit, lead to an increase in public debt, which in turn increases the risk of pressure on money printing. And a larger mass of money causes inflation to rise. A large public finance deficit can lead to higher inflation even if the mass of money does not increase in a given period. This happens when people fear that an increase in the mass of money may occur in the future. These expectations are further reinforced if the accumulation of debt is accompanied by signals that undermine the independence of the central bank and the sense of caring for the value of money.  Secondly, increasing the public finance deficit may or may not stimulate demand, and at the same time - in the long run - inhibits the growth of the productive potential of the economy, because the budget borrows funds from the bank and on the financial market, which could go to enterprises to finance their development. The widening gap between domestic demand and domestic production is either pouring out in the form of more imports, worsening the situation in foreign trade, or it causes inflation to rise. The situation in public finances has been deteriorating since 2001. Public spending in 2001 increased nominally by 12.5 per cent, and in real terms by 6.5 per cent! The economic deficit has reached nearly 4.5 per cent of GDP, which is two and a few times more than in 2000. Last year, it rose to over 5% of GDP, and budget spending was increased in real terms by nearly 4% compared to the very high expenditure of 2001. The previous ustr left a debt to be repaid, which in 1990 exceeded 95 per cent of GDP. Let me remind you that it was a foreign debt incurred in the seventies. Within ten years, it was reduced to about 40 percent of GDP. But this good trend for the country has been reversed. At the end of 2002, public debt, after taking into account the expected payments under guarantees and sureties, had risen to over 47% of GDP. The growing deficit turned into a growing public debt, as the proceeds from privatization fell dramatically. With the rapidly growing borrowing needs of the budget, the government had to borrow money not only at home but also abroad. In 2002, a new debt of almost 2.7 billion was incurred abroad. In addition, a large part of the debt accumulated in the country was actually incurred with foreign investors. Only during 2002, the value of their Treasury securities increased by half, and compared to 2000 it doubled and at the end of 2002 it amounted to over PLN 31 billion. Such increasing borrowing means becoming dependent on external portfolio capital, and this is nervous capital, which easily flows away, raising the interest rates that must be paid for newly incurred debts. This addiction is the result of a large deficit - so it is risky for the country. On the growing debt you have to pay rising interest, which displaces state spending for other purposes or force the government and parliament to raise the tax. We dealt with both of them in 2002.  Last year, debt service costs increased by 15% and reached over PLN 24 billion. At that time, less than PLN 8 billion was spent on public security, and about PLN 5 billion on the justice system. The longer excessive spending is tolerated, the more drastic their subsequent cuts must be. State spending on interest on debt incurred has been growing exponentially for many years, despite the fact that thanks to the main decline in inflation and inflation expectations, interest rates, after which these debts are incurred, have decreased dramatically. From February 2001 to December 2002, the average Yield on Treasury securities fell from more than 15% below 6%. This decline would not have happened if inflation had not been lowered. In 2002 alone, over PLN 1.3 billion was saved. But the total savings are definitely greater. Each percentage point of the decline in treasury yields meant that the costs of servicing the debt incurred in the country in 2001-2002 would be lower by almost PLN 1.6 billion until its repayment. But these figures also show what an increase in the burden threatens the finances of our country if, as a result of the loss of confidence in the investor's economic policy, the interest rate on public debt incurred increases.  In 2002, households and businesses paid about 7 percent, and after adjusting for inflation, more than 5 percent more taxes than in 2001. An additional PLN 10 billion flowed from the pockets of people to the state coffers. The increase in taxes  from an already high level  inhibits the growth of the economy and discourages the expansion of legal employment. 3.3. Benefits of sound public finances in the long and short term. Inflation is reduced to a low level in order to strengthen the long-term development of the economy. If price stability did not bring such benefits, nowhere in the world would try to preserve it. Sick public finances not only increase the risk of rising inflation, but also in other ways harm the long-term development of the country. In the extreme case, a crisis is coming. The bubble is bursting - no one wants to lend to the budget any longer. Everyone is afraid that the state will have nothing to give back and will stop honoring its debts. This expectation becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Unable to borrow any longer, the government must cut public spending heavily, but already in the conditions of the crisis, or drastically raise taxes. borrow. As a result, the country's savings, which could and should finance investments. enterprises and thus serve development, fill the budget gap. History provides more than enough examples of countries that have severely harmed their society due to a lack of budgetary discipline. It is difficult to identify even one country whose long-term development would suffer from an excess of fiscal discipline. Let's focus on the state of public finances in countries that quickly made up for the distance separating them from the wealthiest countries and in those where they lost this distance:  In countries whose economies grew rapidly and started from a low or moderate level of development, the public finance deficit was on average no more than 2% of GDP.  In countries with a similar starting point, whose tranquility was deepening, the deficit was on average about 5-6 per cent of GDP, which is about as much as in Poland today. A large budget deficit also harms development when there is no crisis, because in order to finance the deficit, i.e. excessive spending, the state must constantly Deficit reduction, which is necessary for rapid, long-term development, does not necessarily lead to a temporary slowdown in growth, but on the contrary may cause its immediate acceleration. This possibility stems from more recent economic research, and I say this because, in the popular opinion, reducing the deficit gives long-term benefits, but in the final run it leads to a weakening of demand and growth of the economy. Well, a credible reduction in excessive public spending allows people to expect that in the future taxes will also fall, and thus the part of their income that they can freely dispose of will increase. This expectation leads them to increase their own consumption even before such a tax reduction occurs. Further, thanks to a credible reduction in expenditure and budget deficits, business investment can also increase. Financing the development of companies becomes cheaper, because the state ceases to borrow, and thus to raise interest rates. The ability of companies to invest is also increasing because, as a result of expectations for tax cuts, the worker's pressure to increase wages is weakening. Finally, entrepreneurs can expect that following a permanent reduction in public spending, their tax burden will also be reduced. The fruits of current investments will therefore go to companies to a greater extent. This recipe for accelerating growth is not a pure theory, and it has proven itself in many countries Just for example:  Between 1983 and 1986, Denmark went from a structural deficit, i.e. a deficit that is cleared of the effects of fluctuations in economic activity, exceeding 7% of GDP, to a surplus of 1.5% of GDP. The economy grew in these years at an average rate of almost 4% per year.  In Ireland, the structural deficit was reduced from more than 8% of GDP in 1986 to less than 2% of GDP in 1989. The increase in fiscal discipline was accompanied by an acceleration of economic growth from 0.7 per cent to over 4 per cent.  Recently, Lithuanians have benefited from this recipe for economic success. In 2000, they reduced public spending by nearly 10 percent, bringing the budget deficit down from 6 percent of GDP in 1999 to 2 percent of GDP. Gross domestic product increased by almost 4% in 2000, and growth accelerated to 6% between 2001 and 2002. A decisive and credible reduction in excessive public spending offers a bottom line:  Firstly, by increasing financial capacity and confidence in the future of the consumer and investor, it triggers accelerated economic growth, which in turn increases state tax revenues and reduces public spending related to unemployment or social assistance.  Secondly, it makes it possible to maintain or achieve a low interest rate that must be paid for the public debt incurred. A credible and decisive program to reduce public spending can therefore trigger a positive dynamic, a kind of success wheel. The lack of such a program threatens to push the country into a dynamic of the opposite direction, which in Polish we call a vicious circle. 3.5. Monetary policy summary. Mr. Marshal, High Sejm! Before the political transition began, one of the main problems Polish was the frighteningly fast, destructive rise in prices. In 1989, they increased almost 7.5 times. Since then, we have come a long way. Thanks to a radical stabilisation programme, inflation was reduced to 44 per cent in 1992, to 22 per cent in 1995, to 13 per cent in 1997, to 3.6 per cent in 2001 and to 0.8 per cent in 2002. Monetary policy has contributed to sustainable, rapid development. We already have low inflation  now it needs to be nurtured. Across all indicators, relevant for the well-being of society, this brings us closer to the developed countries. But on one wing it will not fly far. In order for the Polish economy to develop faster in a sustainable way, it is necessary to complete the changes in the political system, which will heal public finances, ensure a wide range of economic freedom and derive politics from enterprises, and thus allow markets to operate, and finally - strengthen the enforcement of the law. Adam Smith, the father of modern economics, stated that: to lead the state out of the state of the deepest barbarism and make it very prosperous, almost nothing is needed except peace, meek taxes and a livable administration of justice, leaving all the rest to the natural course of things. This simple recipe has lost little of its effectiveness. Its implementation would at the same time help to keep inflation low and - in this way, it would further strengthen the long-term development. II 4. Stability of the banking system. Mr Speaker, Honourable Members, The second, basic area of activity of the National Bank of Poland are activities for the stability of the banking sector. Numerous studies conducted in recent years confirm that a stable and developed financial system is one of the foundations for the rapid, long-term development of the economy. A stable financial system is a system resistant to the occurrence of serious disturbances in the performance of its basic functions, such as: mobilization of savings, financing investments or conducting settlements. Building and maintaining the stability of this system are very important, because the financial crisis means a collapse in the growth of the economy. Care for the stability of the financial system is therefore a manifestation of concern for the economic development of the country. A key element of the financial system is the banking sector. In addition to intermediation in converting savings into investments and exercising creditor supervision over enterprises - borrowers, banks form the basis of the system of settling transactions and making payments in the economy. In the case of Polish and other countries of Central and Eastern Europe, as a result of the so far weak development of the capital market, the role of the banking system in the economy is particularly large. In 2002, bank assets accounted for 80% of the assets of the entire financial system. Between 2001 and 2002, the banking system underwent a stability test Polish. After a period of rapid economic development and even faster credit growth, the economic downturn has occurred. It turned out that some of the loans granted during the boom did not sufficiently take into account the risk of deterioration of the situation. Combined with banking supervision activities aimed at showing the actual quality of loans granted by banks, this led to an increase in the share of non-performing receivables in the bank's loan portfolios. In December 2002, it reached 20.7 per cent. It should be emphasized, however, that Polish supervisory regulations regarding the principles of credit classification, creating a kind of early warning system against credit risk, are stricter than used in many countries. If only doubtful and lost loans were taken into account a bank that has been on the balance sheet for no more than one year, the non-performing loan ratio in December 2002 would have accounted for 7.6 per cent of all loans. This is an internationally permissible magnitude. The deterioration in the quality of the loan portfolio did not threaten the stability of the system, as the higher credit risk was completely offset by credit collateral and special-purpose reserves created by banks. The bank's good capital equipment was also a guarantee of the system's security. They are obliged to maintain equity at a level that ensures the security of the accumulated deposit and allows them to cover unexpected losses. The average solvency ratio in December 2002 was 13.7%, compared to the required minimum of 8%. Only in 5 commercial banks and 10 merchant banks its level was lower than this minimum. However, their importance in the entire banking sector is small, and at the same time they are the object of particular interest of banking supervision. An important aspect of the stability of the financial system is the liquidity of banks, i.e. their ability to settle current liabilities. In 2002, banks maintained a high level of liquid assets. Their relation to total assets amounted to approx. 35 per cent and significantly exceeded liabilities due to less stable deposits. In 2002, the National Bank of Polish carried out the following basic activities for the stability of our banking system:  The main form of activity was the continuous supervision of the bank's activities by the General Inspectorate of Banking Supervision. 108 comprehensive inspections and 73 problem inspections were carried out. The scope of the audit has been extended to include the examination of operational risk management of information technology and electronic banking. In order to increase the transparency of banking supervision, the principle of providing banks with information on the assessments granted as a result of studies has been introduced.  The Banking Supervision Commission has adopted the new prudential regulations proposed by the GINB. They allow for a more accurate reflection of the actual risk to which the bank is exposed. The introduction of new rules for calculating regulatory capital should improve the quality of risk management by banks and allow for a more efficient use of their capital.  NBP actively participated in the work on the draft act amending the Banking Law. This amendment provides for changes in prudential regulations, which should strengthen the stability of our banking system.  Every quarter, GINB prepares a report on the assessment of the bank's economic situation, containing comprehensive information on the situation of the banking sector and on possible sources of threats to its stability.  Finally, I would like to say that in June 2002, the Department of the Financial System was established at the National Bank of Poland, which, acting with the General Inspectorate of Banking Supervision, examines the stability of the financial system on an ongoing basis, in particular the banking sector. The Department also conducts analyses of the development of the national financial system. III 5. Management of foreign exchange reserves. Mr Speaker, Honourable Members, The third main area of activity of the National Bank of Poland is the management of official foreign exchange reserves. The National Polish Bank is guided by three principles:  ensuring a high level of security of invested funds;  maintaining the necessary degree of liquidity, i.e. the ability to settle liabilities;  and, while respecting these dwh restrictions, obtaining maximum investment income. Ensuring a high degree of security and liquidity of reserves is provided by the system of limiting investment exposure, regarding the currency structure, credit rating of the issuer of the security in the world and the duration of the deposit. Foreign exchange reserves give the country two kinds of benefits: direct and indirect. Direct benefits consist in achieving income, which goes to the state budget every year. The assessment of the effectiveness of foreign exchange reserve management is made on the basis of the profitability achieved (called current profitability) with the profitability of the so-called pornawcz portfolio (called parity profitability) designated by the NBP Management Board. Within the framework of the adopted security limit, the National Bank of Polish in 2002 shaped the currency structure of reserves assuming the strengthening of the euro against the US dollar. Therefore, the share of the euro was maintained in the small zone of the fluctuation range. The second assumption of the investment strategy in 2002 was to predict a decline in percentages on world markets. In conditions of a decrease in percentages, the prices of fixed-rate securities increase. Therefore, a larger share of these securities was maintained in the structure of reserves. The adoption of these two assumptions turned out to be very beneficial. A doch of investing provisions in the amount of USD 1.1 billion (PLN 4.6 billion) was achieved, and the profitability of foreign exchange reserves in 2002 amounted to 5.5 percent. The indirect benefits of foreign exchange reserves are often forgotten and I would therefore like to remind you of them. In this respect, they resemble health, which is valued when it is lost. Indirect benefits include ensuring the convertibility of national money, the stability of its exchange rate vis-a-vis other currencies, and the financial credibility of the country. These benefits increase with the level of foreign exchange reserves. With the same trade deficit and foreign debt, the size of reserves can determine whether investments in a country's currency are seen as safe. The lack of sufficient reserves with an unfavorable arrangement of other factors can cause capital flight, a drastic increase in percentages and a sharp weakening of the value of domestic money. However, even the largest foreign exchange reserves cannot, of course, replace good economic policies, but they can mitigate the effects of shocks. According to the practice of the central bank, the level of foreign exchange reserves for less developed countries considered safe exceeds the value of six months of imports, and their relation to the country's long-term foreign debt should be at least 100 percent. At the end of 2002, the NBP's official reserve assets, including gold, amounted to USD 29.8 billion and were USD 3.2 billion higher than a year earlier. This increase was mainly due to the strengthening of the euro's exchange rate against the dollar, as part of the reserves was held in euros; further - from the income earned from their investment and, finally, from the repayment by the Ministry of Finance of 1.1 billion dollars, in connection with the loan granted to the government in 2001 for the early and profitable repayment of our debt to Brazil. At the end of 2002, the foreign exchange reserves of the National Bank of Poland covered the value of six and a half months of imports and accounted for about 233 per cent of the foreign debt. It should be emphasized, however, that in a situation of increased risk, foreign investors may also require the return of part of the long-term debt, e.g. by selling Polish Treasury bonds. Therefore, it is also necessary to look at the ratio of foreign exchange reserves to all external debt. In 2002, foreign exchange reserves covered about 37 per cent of this debt. Fortunately, this was clearly more than in countries where currency crises have occurred in recent years, such as Russia, Argentina, Brazil. But in terms of another measure: the ratio of foreign exchange reserves to GDP, Poland with its 16 per cent was at the level of Hungary and much lower than the Czech Republic (34 per cent) and Slovakia (39 per cent). All in all, it can be considered that the foreign exchange reserves of the National Bank of Poland have achieved a certain security prg. Having a strong army deters potential aggressors, ensuring national security. Similarly, having large foreign exchange reserves, they can prevent speculative attacks calculated to weaken the zloty's exchange rate. And the stability of this exchange rate is one of the basic conditions for price stability, which in turn is conducive to good management. The stability of the zloty exchange rate is also important because a large part of loans in banks has been taken out by households and companies in foreign currencies. A sudden weakening of the zloty would mean a big blow for them, because the debt and interest expressed in zlotys would increase accordingly. The importance of foreign exchange reserves will increase in the near future. Our country is waiting on the way to the euro two years of experience under the European exchange rate mechanism ERM2, in order to maintain the exchange rate in the fluctuation range currently we do not have a range - central bank interventions on foreign exchange market. Reliable and therefore effective interventions will require a high level of foreign exchange reserves. Finally, large foreign exchange reserves strengthen the country's credibility, which enables the state and private economic operators to borrow foreign loans at lower interest rates than when the level of reserves is perceived as too low. And this results in savings in the costs of servicing foreign debt reaching hundreds of a million zlotys. From this, of course, it follows that the excessive depletion of these reserves could cost our country a lot. IV 6. Internal reforms in the NBP. Mr Speaker, High House. The National Bank of Polish like other central banks, is strengthening its analytical divisions.
